Thank you for submitting your article "Formin-2 drives polymerisation of actin filaments enabling segregation of apicoplasts and cytokinesis in P. falciparum" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by Anna Akhmanova as the Senior and Reviewing Editor, and three reviewers. The following individual involved in the review of your submission has agreed to reveal their identity: Tobias Spielmann (Reviewer #1).

The reviewers have discussed the reviews with one another and the Reviewing Editor has drafted this decision to help you prepare a revised submission.

This paper employs chromobodies to document the localization and dynamics of the actin cytoskeleton in Plasmodium and Toxoplasma and provides insight into the function of formin in regulating the formation of different actin structures in these parasites. Overall, the reviewers were positive about the quality of the data and the strength of the conclusions. Therefore, the reviewers agreed that it was not necessary to perform additional experiments, but that the paper would benefit from improving the writing and the presentation of the data. We include below the individual reviews and hope that you will finding them helpful when revising your paper.

Reviewer #1:

Filamentous actin has been notoriously difficult to detect in malaria parasites. In this paper the authors use chromobodies to visualise F-actin in live malaria parasites. They validate the observed structures to be F-actin using CytD and Jaspla and in a conditional actin KO. Next they generated a conditional Formin-2 KO and used the actin chromobody to assess the impact on actin. This permitted them to nicely link phenotypes of the Formin-2 KO with changes in F-actin pools in the cell. This is most convincing with the apicoplast which shows a segregation phenotype (fitting with the phenotype of the conditional actin KO that the authors previously showed in Das et al., 2017). The manuscript also shows that knocking out Formin-2 leads to loss of the F-actin network around the food vacuole. This network is present in late stage malaria parasites and likely is equivalent of the intravacuolar actin network in Toxoplasma parasites. The dependence of this network on Formin-2 is in contrast to the situation in T. gondii, where this network is dependent on a third formin that is not present in malaria parasites. These findings are shown in the last part of the manuscript where the authors analyse F-actin in a conditional Formin-2 KO in Toxoplasma. In part this overlaps with data from a recent report in eLife (Tosetti et al., 2019) that also used the actin chromobody of the authors of the present manuscript. Interestingly, the work here indicates bi-directional F-actin flows along the parasite periphery whereas the previous report by Tosetti et al., indicated unidirectional flow toward the basal end.

Together with other work, this paper leaves us with a good picture which formin drives different actin-mediated processes in plasmodium and toxoplasma parasites. It convincingly shows that Formin-2 plays a central role for most actin-dependent processes in malaria blood stages (including the functions of Formin3 in T. gondii) but not the invasion functions which are controlled by Formin-1. A highlight of the paper is the visualisation of F-actin in living malaria parasites, which is also demonstrated in a number of nice time-lapse movies. The actin chromobody will be an excellent tool for further functional studies in this parasite. Overall this is technically very challenging work that includes multiple conditional knock outs and is experimentally sound.

The only larger concern I have is the cytokinesis phenotype in the Formin-2 KO (but this may be solved by simply changing the text to allow other options). Can the authors exclude that other phenotypes in later trophozoites or early schizonts contribute to the phenotype? Many different cellular defects could lead to the reduced number of nuclei in Figure 6A. In fact, this figure most likely indicates a general developmental delay rather than a specific phenotype. Do the 'slower' cells with less than 5 nuclei in Figure 6A still make it to egress? Or do they have other defects that make them arrest earlier? If they do not reach the late schizont, it may not only be a cell division phenotype. Was Figure 6E done with purified late stages or with all parasites on/off RAP?

The subsequent experiments (Figure 6B etc.) are then done with purified late stage parasites which consists of the subfraction that makes it to that stage (maybe those parasites where Formin-2 levels dropped more slowly after excision of the gene?). These experiments are important, as they show that the merozoites produced from this subfraction are still invasive and show that the Formin-1 dependent functions are not affected. The experiments are also consistent with the author's conclusion that this signifies a role of Formin-2 in 'coordinate cytokinesis'. However, it does not exclude that Formin-2 may have earlier function in schizogony. Unless all cells on RAP eventually make it to that stage, this may be just one of the phenotypes. This should be discussed.

Reviewer #2:

This is in principle a well performed study investigating actin dynamics in P. falciparum blood stages and T. gondii using a fluorescent antibody against actin filaments and a focus on the actin polymerizing protein Formin-2. The authors confirm and expand on recent work published in eLife and elsewhere introducing the chromobody, showing the importance of three different formins on actin polymerization in T. gondii as well as the finding that actin is important for apicoplast division. There is quite some overlap on the Formin-2 part with the recent paper from the Soldati group, but this should be covered by the scoop protection mechanism offered by eLife. The authors do a good job dissecting the differences in the roles of actin in Plasmodium and Toxoplasma.

This paper improves on the previously published eLife article of the same lab by examining for the first time actin dynamics with a chromobody in P. falciparum and by providing enhanced image analysis, which led to the discovery of a bidirectional cytoplasmic flow of actin filaments.

I don't have suggestions for additional experiments but maybe the authors can reflect on/discuss the following points:

It would improve reading experience if the movies would be somehow fused into fewer total movies, if possible – e.g. Video 1, Video 2, Video 3 and Video 4 could be put back to back of each other into a single file.

Can the structures visualized by the chromobody be bleached to investigate their turnover?

Does the bi-directional flow observed here compare with the recently reported actin flow in oocysts by the Heisenberg lab (2019)? How does this fit to the data recently published in eLife, where actin flows only from front of T. gondii to their back?

Reviewer #3:

This manuscript describes a technological breakthrough in the study of P. falciparum, an organism of great clinical significance, as well as reveals novel details on this organism's actin cytoskeleton, and draws parallels and distinctions for the roles Formin-2 in this organism and the distantly related T. gondii. This appears to be the second round of reviews for this manuscript, although this is my first viewing of the manuscript. Overall, I am satisfied with the rigor shown, and with the major conclusions that the authors draw. In particular, I am comfortable with the authors' demonstration that the chromobodies (CB's) are indeed faithfully decorating actin-based structures, and based on their sensitivity to CytoD, agree that these structures are likely F-actin-based. As outlined below, my main concerns regarding this work are the specific wordings used at some places in the manuscript regarding "dynamics", some omissions or gaps in the figure descriptions that cause confusion, and some missing information regarding the phylogenetic analysis.

1) The authors frequently use the term "dynamics" when describing actin-based structures. Based on their data, I would agree that many of the structures they view are dynamic in the sense that are mobile (e.g. subsection “F-actin in gametocytes”). However, "dynamic" with regards to actin also often refers to the degree to which the actin filaments undergo turnover (rounds of polymerization and depolymerization). The authors should review their text and edit where it needs to be made clear which type of dynamics they are discussing. Related to this, the authors claim to show that "islands of F-actin are stabilized upon jasplakinolide treatment (+JAS) (Figure 1C)", but this is documented only by a still image with large fluorescent bodies. The authors cite Video 3, but there is no +JAS movie on that video, only control and +CytoD. I agree that the authors could interpret their result as being consistent with stabilization of F-actin, but without showing that there is reduced turnover of actin in these structures, they should hedge on their wording some.

2) I also strongly recommend the authors supplement some of their figures/figure legends to help the reader better interpret the data. In particular:

For Figure 2Bii, the legend explains the significance of the bottom panels, but not the top four panels. Are they different time points?

For Figure 3G, the figure legend should provide some more information to help the reader understand the model. That is, "syn", "loxPint", and "WR" should be defined. It is a very elegant construct but requires a lot of flipping back and forth between the legend, text, and methods to deconstruct what is going on.

For Figure 3H, it currently gives the impression that Integrant 1 and Integrant 2 are being analyzed, when in fact it is transformant 1 and transformant 2 that are being analyzed, using a PCR reaction that probes for integration or the endogenous locus. I would suggest clarifying the labels, such as replacing "Integrant" and "Endogen." with "PCR(Int)" and "PCR(End)" (with clarifications in the legend), and add the label "Transformant:" to the left of "1 2 1 2" above the gels.

claims.claim: Conditional disruption of Formin-2 results in a loss of an intracellular F-actin polymerisation centre in T. gondii.
claims.source: Conditional disruption of Formin-2 not only results in a complete abrogation of actin dynamics in P. falciparum and a loss of an intracellular F-actin polymerisation centre in T. gondii, it also leads to defects in apicoplast inheritance in both genera.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data.

claims.claim: Conditional disruption of Formin-2 leads to defects in apicoplast inheritance in both P. falciparum and T. gondii.
claims.source: Conditional disruption of Formin-2 not only results in a complete abrogation of actin dynamics in P. falciparum and a loss of an intracellular F-actin polymerisation centre in T. gondii, it also leads to defects in apicoplast inheritance in both genera.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data.

claims.claim: Formin-2 is additionally involved in completion of cytokinesis in P. falciparum, in contrast to Toxoplasma.
claims.source: In contrast to Toxoplasma, Formin-2 is additionally involved in completion of cytokinesis in P. falciparum.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data.

claims.claim: Actin-chromobodies were expressed under control of the heat shock protein 86 (hsp86) promoter to obtain expression throughout the 48 hr asexual life cycle.
claims.source: Actin-chromobodies (Chromotek) were expressed under control of the heat shock protein 86 (hsp86) promoter (Crabb and Cowman, 1996) to obtain expression throughout the 48 hr asexual life cycle.
claims.evidence: This is a methodological detail supported by citation to Crabb and Cowman, 1996.

claims.claim: Parasites stably expressing actin-chromobodies tagged with emerald or halo tags were successfully generated.
claims.source: We succeeded in generating parasites stably expressing actin-chromobodies tagged either with the emerald tag (CB-EME) (Figure 1B), or the halo tag (CB-HALO) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), indicating that the expression of these constructs does not have a major deleterious impact on the fitness of P. falciparum as previously reported for Toxoplasma (Periz et al., 2017) and other eukaryotes.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citation to Periz et al., 2017.

claims.claim: Expression of actin-chromobodies does not have a major deleterious impact on the fitness of P. falciparum.
claims.source: We succeeded in generating parasites stably expressing actin-chromobodies tagged either with the emerald tag (CB-EME) (Figure 1B), or the halo tag (CB-HALO) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), indicating that the expression of these constructs does not have a major deleterious impact on the fitness of P. falciparum as previously reported for Toxoplasma (Periz et al., 2017) and other eukaryotes.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from successful generation of stable parasites and supported by citation to Periz et al., 2017.

claims.claim: Dynamic filamentous structures were evident in both CB-EME and CB-HALO expressing parasites throughout the 48 hr asexual life cycle and in gametocytes.
claims.source: Dynamic filamentous structures were evident in both CB-EME (Figure 1) and CB-HALO expressing parasites (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) throughout the 48 hr asexual life cycle (see also Videos 1, 2, 3 and 4) and in gametocytes (Video 5).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures and videos.

claims.claim: Filamentous structures labeled by chromobodies could be completely disrupted by treatment with cytochalasin-D.
claims.source: These structures could be completely disrupted by treatment with F-actin destabilising drug cytochalasin-D (30 min, final concentration 1 µM) or stabilised by addition of the depolymerisation inhibitor Jasplakinolide (JAS) (30 min, final concentration 1 µM) (Figure 1C bottom panels and Video 3), demonstrating that chromobodies bind F-actin structures in P. falciparum.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and Video 3.

claims.claim: Filamentous structures labeled by chromobodies could be stabilised by addition of Jasplakinolide.
claims.source: These structures could be completely disrupted by treatment with F-actin destabilising drug cytochalasin-D (30 min, final concentration 1 µM) or stabilised by addition of the depolymerisation inhibitor Jasplakinolide (JAS) (30 min, final concentration 1 µM) (Figure 1C bottom panels and Video 3), demonstrating that chromobodies bind F-actin structures in P. falciparum.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and Video 3.

claims.claim: Chromobodies bind F-actin structures in P. falciparum.
claims.source: These structures could be completely disrupted by treatment with F-actin destabilising drug cytochalasin-D (30 min, final concentration 1 µM) or stabilised by addition of the depolymerisation inhibitor Jasplakinolide (JAS) (30 min, final concentration 1 µM) (Figure 1C bottom panels and Video 3), demonstrating that chromobodies bind F-actin structures in P. falciparum.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the effects of F-actin modulating drugs on chromobody-labeled structures.

claims.claim: Expression of CB-EME resulted in a better signal-to-noise ratio than CB-HALO.
claims.source: However, while both chromobody versions labelled similar structures, we found that expression of CB-EME resulted in a better signal-to-noise ratio. This is probably because no permeable, fluorescent ligand needs to be added for visualisation.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the study with a speculative explanation.

claims.claim: Some F-actin structures were highly dynamic, changing within time-scales of seconds, while other structures appeared stable over tens of seconds.
claims.source: Some F-actin structures were highly dynamic, changing within a time-scales of seconds, while other structures appeared stable over tens of seconds (Video 3, see also quantifications below).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in videos and quantifications.

claims.claim: F-actin rich islands at the periphery of ~60% of ring and early trophozoite stage parasites were observed.
claims.source: On observing chromobody-expressing parasites during ring and early trophozoite stages we noted F-actin rich islands at the periphery of ~60% parasites (n = 50) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and Video 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and Video 2.

claims.claim: Peripheral F-actin accumulations were highly dynamic, changing in order of seconds.
claims.source: These F-actin accumulations were highly dynamic, changing in order of seconds (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and Video 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and Video 2.

claims.claim: Upon treatment with cytochalasin-D, the peripheral, highly dynamic accumulations completely disappeared.
claims.source: Upon treatment with the F-actin depolymerising drug cytochalasin-D (30 min, final concentration of 1 µM) the peripheral, highly dynamic accumulations completely disappeared (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B lower panel), while the multi-lobed structures of the parasite were not disrupted (Video 6).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B and Video 6.

claims.claim: The multi-lobed structures of the parasite were not disrupted by cytochalasin-D treatment.
claims.source: Upon treatment with the F-actin depolymerising drug cytochalasin-D (30 min, final concentration of 1 µM) the peripheral, highly dynamic accumulations completely disappeared (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B lower panel), while the multi-lobed structures of the parasite were not disrupted (Video 6).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Video 6.

claims.claim: Jasplakinolide disrupted peripheral F-actin and resulted in formation of stable thick filaments.
claims.source: The F-actin stabilising drug jasplakinolide also disrupted peripheral F-actin and resulted in formation of stable thick filaments (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B lower panel), implying the requirement of dynamic regulation of F-actin for peripheral F-actin accumulations.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claims.claim: Dynamic regulation of F-actin is required for peripheral F-actin accumulations.
claims.source: The F-actin stabilising drug jasplakinolide also disrupted peripheral F-actin and resulted in formation of stable thick filaments (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B lower panel), implying the requirement of dynamic regulation of F-actin for peripheral F-actin accumulations.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the effects of jasplakinolide on peripheral F-actin.

claims.claim: Compound-1 and -2 are reversible inhibitors of protein kinase G that stall schizont development at very mature stages without allowing egress.
claims.source: Reversible inhibitors of protein kinase G, Compound-1 and −2, stall schizont development at very mature stages without allowing them to undergo egress (Collins et al., 2013b).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Collins et al., 2013b.

claims.claim: Upon washing away Compound-2, parasites egressed normally with the concomitant appearance of F-actin accumulation at the apical tip of the parasite.
claims.source: Upon washing away Compound-2, the parasites egressed normally with the concomitant appearance of F-actin accumulation at the apical tip of the parasite (Figure 1D, Video 4).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and Video 4.

claims.claim: Cytochalasin-D treatment allowed normal egress of parasites but completely abrogated F-actin polymerisation at the apical tip following egress.
claims.source: Cytochalasin-D treatment (30 min, final concentration 1 µM) allowed normal egress of parasites, as previously observed (Weiss et al., 2015), but completely abrogated F-actin polymerisation at the apical tip following egress (Figure 1D,+CytoD).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and citation to Weiss et al., 2015.

claims.claim: F-actin accumulates just behind the RON4 ring in invading merozoites.
claims.source: Furthermore, we performed IFA on invading merozoites using rhoptry neck protein 4 (RON4) as a junctional marker. We verified that F-actin accumulates just behind the RON4 ring (Figure 1E) confirming previous observations made with an antibody preferentially recognising F-actin in P. falciparum (Riglar et al., 2011; Angrisano et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E and citations to Riglar et al., 2011; Angrisano et al., 2012.

claims.claim: Gametocytes express both PfACT1 and actin-2.
claims.source: In contrast to asexual parasites, gametocytes express both PfACT1 and actin-2, and exhibit F-actin staining along the length of the parasite and at the tips (Hliscs et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Hliscs et al., 2015.

claims.claim: Gametocytes exhibit F-actin staining along the length of the parasite and at the tips.
claims.source: In contrast to asexual parasites, gametocytes express both PfACT1 and actin-2, and exhibit F-actin staining along the length of the parasite and at the tips (Hliscs et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Hliscs et al., 2015.

claims.claim: CB-EME expression in gametocytes showed intense dynamic F-actin structures at their tips and running along the whole body of the cell.
claims.source: Upon expression of CB-EME, gametocytes showed intense dynamic F-actin structures at their tips and running along the whole body of the cell (Figure 1F and Video 5).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F and Video 5.

claims.claim: The dynamic F-actin network in gametocytes appears very similar to the one reported by Hliscs et al. (2015), which lies beneath the IMC of the gametocyte.
claims.source: Importantly, this dynamic network appears very similar to the one reported by Hliscs et al. (2015), which has been shown to lie beneath the IMC of the gametocyte.
claims.evidence: This is supported by comparison to prior work cited (Hliscs et al., 2015).

claims.claim: Actin-chromobodies do not distinguish between PfACT1 and actin-2.
claims.source: It is important to note that actin-chromobodies do not distinguish between PfACT1 and actin-2 and therefore the observed filaments could potentially be composed of both proteins.
claims.evidence: This is a limitation of the chromobody technology stated by the authors.

claims.claim: During the gametocyte stage, F-actin forms a dynamic and extensive network that passes through the whole cell and is enriched at the tips of the parasite.
claims.source: We therefore confirm previous data obtained with antibodies directed against F-actin (Hliscs et al., 2015) and show that during the gametocyte stage, F-actin forms a dynamic and extensive network that passes through the whole cell and is enriched at the tips of the parasite.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citation to Hliscs et al., 2015.

claims.claim: Super-resolution microscopy revealed a complex F-actin network in P. falciparum parasites.
claims.source: For better visualisation of F-actin structures, we used super-resolution microscopy (SR-SIM) which revealed a complex F-actin network in these parasites (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: F-actin was prominent around the FV of the parasite.
claims.source: Interestingly, F-actin was prominent around the FV of the parasite (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1, see also Figure 2—figure supplement 2 lower left panel), which is also the basal end of the newly-formed daughter parasites during the final stages of cytokinesis.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claims.claim: The FV is at the basal end of the newly-formed daughter parasites during the final stages of cytokinesis.
claims.source: Interestingly, F-actin was prominent around the FV of the parasite (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1, see also Figure 2—figure supplement 2 lower left panel), which is also the basal end of the newly-formed daughter parasites during the final stages of cytokinesis.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about P. falciparum biology.

claims.claim: When the actin-chromobody-labelled network was co-stained with an antibody raised against parasite actin, similar structures as seen with chromobody were apparent.
claims.source: When we co-stained the actin-chromobody-labelled network with an antibody raised against parasite actin (Angrisano et al., 2012), similar structures as seen with chromobody were apparent (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and citation to Angrisano et al., 2012.

claims.claim: The staining of chromobody and actin antibody was not identical, perhaps due to the masking of antibody binding sites by other binding proteins.
claims.source: The staining was however not identical perhaps due to the masking of antibody binding sites by other binding proteins, which was also observed previously for T. gondii actin (Periz et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is a speculative explanation supported by citation to Periz et al., 2017.

claims.claim: A Pearson's R value of 0.6 was obtained for co-localisation of the CB-EME signal with that of the actin-antibody.
claims.source: Upon quantification of co-localisation of the CB-EME signal with that of the actin-antibody, we obtained a Pearson's R value of 0.6, in comparison to R values of 0.2 when the CBEME signal was tested for co-localisation with the DAPI signal.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data from co-localisation analysis.

claims.claim: IMC markers GAP45 and MTIP showed normal staining in CB-EME expressing parasites.
claims.source: IMC markers GAP45 and MTIP showed normal staining in CB-EME expressing parasites (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: Expression of chromobodies does not cause significant phenotypic effects and allows reliable labelling of the F-actin cytoskeleton.
claims.source: Together, our data show that expression of chromobodies does not cause significant phenotypic effects and allow reliable labelling of the F-actin cytoskeleton.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented.

claims.claim: Upon disruption of PfACT1, CB-EME and CB-HALO labelled F-actin structures completely disappeared in late trophozoites and schizonts.
claims.source: Upon induction with RAP in 1h-old ring stages, CB-EME (Figure 2, Video 7) and CB-HALO (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C) labelled F-actin structures completely disappeared in late trophozoites and schizonts and closely resembled parasites treated with cytochalasin-D (Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures and videos.

claims.claim: PfACT1-disrupted parasites could not invade new erythrocytes.
claims.source: As previously reported (Das et al., 2017), PfACT1-disrupted parasites could not invade new erythrocytes (Figure 2B(ii)).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B(ii) and citation to Das et al., 2017.

claims.claim: A ≈ 10x reduction in emerald signal was observed upon disruption of PfACT1.
claims.source: We observed a ≈ 10x reduction in emerald signal upon disruption of PfACT1 (Figure 2C), which could be due to the proteasomal degradation of actin-chromobodies, when they are not bound to actin, as was seen by others for a different chromobody (Tang et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C and citation to Tang et al., 2016.

claims.claim: Apicoplast inheritance depends on PfACT1.
claims.source: We previously reported that apicoplast inheritance depends on PfACT1 (Das et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Das et al., 2017.

claims.claim: Apicoplasts are in close proximity with F-actin structures.
claims.source: In order to determine the localisation of F-actin during apicoplast segregation we used deconvolution microscopy on fixed parasites stained with the apicoplast marker CPN60, which revealed apicoplasts to be in close proximity with F-actin structures (Figure 2D,E; Figure 2—figure supplement 1B lower panel).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claims.claim: A Pearson's R value of 0.4 was obtained for colocalisation of the apicoplast(s) signal with the CB-EME channel.
claims.source: A Pearson's R value of 0.4 was obtained for colocalisation of the apicoplast(s) signal with the CB-EME channel in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B lower panel, as compared to 0.1 with the DAPI channel.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data from co-localisation analysis.

claims.claim: 75% ± 7% of apicoplasts lie apposed to the F-actin network.
claims.source: We also scored for individual apicoplast signals which are proximal to the F-actin network (example shown in Figure 2E) and found 75% ± 7% apicoplasts to lie apposed to the F-actin network (N = 445).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data from quantification.

claims.claim: Upon disruption of PfACT1, a defect in apicoplast segregation was apparent.
claims.source: Upon disruption of PfACT1, a defect in apicoplast segregation was apparent (Figure 2D PfAct1cKO), which recapitulated the phenotype previously observed (Das et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D and citation to Das et al., 2017.

claims.claim: No obvious defects in mitochondria segregation could be detected in PfACT1-disrupted parasites.
claims.source: In contrast, no obvious defects in mitochondria segregation could be detected in PfACT1-disrupted parasites (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and Video 7) as previously reported (Das et al., 2017), implying that unlike apicoplasts, mitochondria do not require F-actin for migration into daughter cells.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and Video 7, and citation to Das et al., 2017.

claims.claim: Mitochondria do not require F-actin for migration into daughter cells.
claims.source: In contrast, no obvious defects in mitochondria segregation could be detected in PfACT1-disrupted parasites (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and Video 7) as previously reported (Das et al., 2017), implying that unlike apicoplasts, mitochondria do not require F-actin for migration into daughter cells.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the lack of mitochondrial segregation defects in PfACT1-disrupted parasites.

claims.claim: Stable time-averaged F-actin peaks were observed, which could be easily distinguished from background and from the signal in PfACT1KO parasites.
claims.source: Stable time-averaged F-actin peaks were observed, which could be easily distinguished from background and from the signal in PfACT1KO parasites (Figure 2F, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claims.claim: The highest time-averaged intensity peaks were observed around the food vacuole.
claims.source: We observed the highest time-averaged intensity peaks around the food vacuole, as also noted by super-resolution microscopy (Figure 2—figure supplement 2, lower left panel).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: PfFRM1 has been localised to the invasion junction.
claims.source: Previously, PfFRM1 has been localised to the invasion junction and PfFRM2 to the cytosol (Baum et al., 2008b).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Baum et al., 2008b.

claims.claim: PfFRM2 has been localised to the cytosol.
claims.source: Previously, PfFRM1 has been localised to the invasion junction and PfFRM2 to the cytosol (Baum et al., 2008b).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Baum et al., 2008b.

claims.claim: Formin-2 is the main nucleator of F-actin during intracellular parasite development.
claims.source: Since we observed the intracellular F-actin network in the cytosol, we speculated that Formin-2 is the main nucleator of F-actin during intracellular parasite development.
claims.evidence: This is a speculation based on the observed localisation of F-actin and Formin-2.

claims.claim: Formins possess a formin homology (FH) one and an FH2 domain, which nucleate actin monomers as well as elongate unbranched F-actin by continuous processive binding to the barbed end of the filament.
claims.source: Formins possess a formin homology (FH) one and an FH2 domain, which nucleate actin monomers as well as elongate unbranched F-actin by continuous processive binding to the barbed end of the filament (Courtemanche, 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Courtemanche, 2018.

claims.claim: In a previous report, only FH1/FH2 domains were described for apicomplexan formins.
claims.source: In a previous report (Baum et al., 2008b), only FH1/FH2 domains were described for apicomplexan formins.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Baum et al., 2008b.

claims.claim: Tetratricopeptide repeat (TPR) domains were found in both PfFRM1 and TgFRM1.
claims.source: Here, we queried for presence of known PFAM domains using NCBI conserved domain search and in addition to FH1/FH2, found tetratricopeptide repeat (TPR) domains in both PfFRM1 and TgFRM1, while a PTEN C2-like domain was recognised in PfFRM2 and TgFRM2 (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by bioinformatic analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: A PTEN C2-like domain was recognised in PfFRM2 and TgFRM2.
claims.source: Here, we queried for presence of known PFAM domains using NCBI conserved domain search and in addition to FH1/FH2, found tetratricopeptide repeat (TPR) domains in both PfFRM1 and TgFRM1, while a PTEN C2-like domain was recognised in PfFRM2 and TgFRM2 (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by bioinformatic analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: Formin-1 and Formin-2 with different N-terminal domains diverged early in evolution and different domain organisations have been retained for different functions.
claims.source: This led us to hypothesise that Formin-1 and Formin-2 with different N-terminal domains diverged early in evolution and different domain organisations have been retained for different functions.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the bioinformatic findings.

claims.claim: Formin-2-like sequences are found in a different clade from Formin-1-like sequences.
claims.source: We queried for FH2-domain containing proteins from various apicomplexans and found that Formin-2-like sequences are found in a different clade from Formin-1-like sequences (Figure 3B), as also previously noted (Baum et al., 2008b).
claims.evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 3B and citation to Baum et al., 2008b.

claims.claim: The PTEN-C2-domain (or a diverged PTEN-C2 domain) was found only in Formin-2-like sequences.
claims.source: Strikingly, the PTEN-C2-domain (or a diverged PTEN-C2 domain) was found only in Formin-2-like sequences (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by bioinformatic analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: PTEN-C2 domains are important for membrane recruitment.
claims.source: Interestingly, PTEN-C2 domains are important for membrane recruitment (Das et al., 2003) and a class II rice Formin uses this domain to be recruited to chloroplast membranes (Zhang et al., 2011), leading us to hypothesise that a similar mechanism operates for apicoplast recruitment of Formin-2 sequences in apicomplexans.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Das et al., 2003; Zhang et al., 2011.

claims.claim: A class II rice Formin uses the PTEN-C2 domain to be recruited to chloroplast membranes.
claims.source: Interestingly, PTEN-C2 domains are important for membrane recruitment (Das et al., 2003) and a class II rice Formin uses this domain to be recruited to chloroplast membranes (Zhang et al., 2011), leading us to hypothesise that a similar mechanism operates for apicoplast recruitment of Formin-2 sequences in apicomplexans.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2011.

claims.claim: A similar mechanism to rice Formin operates for apicoplast recruitment of Formin-2 sequences in apicomplexans.
claims.source: Interestingly, PTEN-C2 domains are important for membrane recruitment (Das et al., 2003) and a class II rice Formin uses this domain to be recruited to chloroplast membranes (Zhang et al., 2011), leading us to hypothesise that a similar mechanism operates for apicoplast recruitment of Formin-2 sequences in apicomplexans.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the similarity of PTEN-C2 domains in rice Formin and apicomplexan Formin-2.

claims.claim: TgFRM2 was found to be localised adjacent to apicoplast(s).
claims.source: Upon co-staining with the anti-apicoplast antibody G2-Trx (Biddau and Sheiner, unpublished), we found TgFRM2 to be localised adjacent to apicoplast(s) (Figure 3E), which was confirmed by super-resolution microscopy (Figure 3F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E and 3F.

claims.claim: 30% of apicoplasts partially colocalised and 58% apicoplasts were adjacent to and in contact with the TgFRM2 signal.
claims.source: Upon quantification of co-localisation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), we found 30% apicoplasts partially colocalised and 58% apicoplasts adjacent to and in contact with the TgFRM2 signal (n = 142).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: PfFRM2 showed a punctate pattern within cells.
claims.source: PfFRM2 showed a punctate pattern within cells (Figure 3I).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3I.

claims.claim: PfFRM2 localises in close proximity to apicoplasts throughout the 48 hr Plasmodium blood stage life-cycle.
claims.source: Next, we checked for PfFRM2 localisation in relation to apicoplasts and observed a close proximity of the apicoplasts with most of the PfFRM2 punctae throughout the 48 hr Plasmodium blood stage life-cycle (Figure 3J), which was confirmed by super-resolution microscopy (Figure 3K).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3J and 3K.

claims.claim: A Pearson's R value of 0.55 ± 0.2 was obtained for co-localisation of the apicoplast signal with that of the formin punctae.
claims.source: Upon quantification of co-localisation of the apicoplast signal with that of the formin punctae, we obtained a Pearson's R value of 0.55 ± 0.2 (N = 4), the high variance implying that the close proximity of the apicoplasts to Formin-2 may be dynamic.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data from co-localisation analysis.

claims.claim: The close proximity of the apicoplasts to Formin-2 may be dynamic.
claims.source: Upon quantification of co-localisation of the apicoplast signal with that of the formin punctae, we obtained a Pearson's R value of 0.55 ± 0.2 (N = 4), the high variance implying that the close proximity of the apicoplasts to Formin-2 may be dynamic.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the high variance in the Pearson's R value.

claims.claim: Excision of the pffrm2 locus was confirmed by diagnostic PCR.
claims.source: Excision was determined by diagnostic PCR of the genomic locus (Figure 4B) and fitness of the PfFRM2 conditional knock out (cKO) was measured by a growth curve which showed significant loss of viability (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: Fitness of the PfFRM2 conditional knock out (cKO) showed significant loss of viability.
claims.source: Excision was determined by diagnostic PCR of the genomic locus (Figure 4B) and fitness of the PfFRM2 conditional knock out (cKO) was measured by a growth curve which showed significant loss of viability (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: Loss of PfFRM2 protein was ~90% as determined by Western blot.
claims.source: Loss of protein was ~90% (averaged from three independent experiments) as determined by Western blot (Figure 4D) and was confirmed by IFA (Figure 4E), which indicated a loss of protein in ~95% parasites (N = 350).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: Loss of PfFRM2 protein was confirmed by IFA, which indicated a loss of protein in ~95% parasites.
claims.source: Loss of protein was ~90% (averaged from three independent experiments) as determined by Western blot (Figure 4D) and was confirmed by IFA (Figure 4E), which indicated a loss of protein in ~95% parasites (N = 350).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claims.claim: Giemsa stained PfFRM2 cKO parasites were dysmorphic with apparent inclusions of haemoglobin.
claims.source: Giemsa stained PfFRM2 cKO parasites were dysmorphic with apparent inclusions of haemoglobin (Figure 4F, red arrows).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F.

claims.claim: The number of parasites with normally segregated apicoplasts was significantly reduced in PfFRM2 cKO parasites, with a high percentage of cells showing collapsed or morphologically aberrant apicoplasts.
claims.source: The number of parasites with normally segregated apicoplasts was significantly reduced, with a high percentage of cells showing collapsed or morphologically aberrant apicoplasts (Figure 4G,H).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4G and 4H.

claims.claim: A range of apicoplast phenotypes was evident in PfFRM2 cKO parasites, from totally collapsed, intermediate to apparently normal.
claims.source: A range of apicoplast phenotypes was evident, from totally collapsed, intermediate to apparently normal (Figure 4G,H).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4G and 4H.

claims.claim: Isopentenyl pyrophosphate (IPP) did not improve viability of PfFRM2 cKO parasites.

results.result: Actin-binding chromobodies (CB-EME and CB-HALO) were successfully expressed in P. falciparum throughout the 48 hr asexual life cycle, enabling visualization of dynamic F-actin structures that could be chemically modulated with cytochalasin-D and jasplakinolide without causing major fitness defects.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C5, C28-C30, C77-C85 collectively demonstrate successful expression and validation of chromobodies as F-actin sensors. The data show drug-responsive F-actin structures (C29-C30, C81-C82), stable parasite lines (C78-C79), and dynamic filaments throughout the life cycle (C28, C80, C85), with CB-EME providing better signal-to-noise ratio than CB-HALO (C84). This represents a major technical achievement enabling subsequent analyses.

results.result: Conditional disruption of PfACT1 resulted in complete loss of CB-EME/CB-HALO labeled F-actin structures, defects in apicoplast segregation (with 75±7% of apicoplasts normally apposed to F-actin in wild-type), and invasion defects, while mitochondrial segregation remained unaffected.
results.evaluation: Claims C110-C119 provide converging evidence validating chromobodies as authentic F-actin sensors. Loss of F-actin structures upon PfACT1 disruption (C110), correlation with known invasion defects (C111), proximity of apicoplasts to F-actin (C114-C116), and selective effect on apicoplast but not mitochondria (C117-C119) are well-supported by experimental data and consistent with prior work (Das et al., 2017).

results.result: F-actin polymerizes at the apical tip of merozoites immediately after egress (in 56±9% of egressed merozoites), accumulating just behind the RON4 junction marker, and this polymerization is completely prevented by cytochalasin-D treatment while egress proceeds normally.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C33, C93-C95, C199-C201 demonstrate for the first time the temporal and spatial dynamics of apical F-actin polymerization during invasion. The data show timing (immediately post-egress, C31, C93), localization (behind RON4 ring, C33, C95), drug sensitivity (C32, C94), and quantification (56±9%, C31). The inference that early signaling triggers polymerization (C201) is reasonable but speculative.

results.result: Bioinformatic analysis revealed that apicomplexan Formin-2 sequences contain a PTEN-C2-like domain (found only in Formin-2-like sequences across apicomplexans) that is used for chloroplast membrane recruitment in rice Formin, suggesting a similar mechanism for apicoplast recruitment in apicomplexans.
results.evaluation: Claims C127-C134 present bioinformatic findings showing PTEN-C2 domains in PfFRM2/TgFRM2 (C127-C128), phylogenetic separation of Formin-2 sequences (C130-C131), and functional precedent in rice (C132-C133). The hypothesis of apicoplast recruitment (C134) is reasonable given the rice precedent but remains to be experimentally validated. The bioinformatic analysis is sound and the inference is logical.

results.result: Formin-2 localizes in close proximity to apicoplasts in both P. falciparum and T. gondii throughout the life cycle, with PfFRM2 showing punctate patterns (Pearson's R=0.55±0.2 with apicoplasts) and TgFRM2 showing 30% partial colocalization and 58% adjacent contact with apicoplasts.
results.evaluation: Claims C72, C135-C140 demonstrate conserved Formin-2 localization near apicoplasts in both organisms using multiple imaging approaches (IFA, super-resolution). Quantification shows substantial proximity (C136, C139) with high variance suggesting dynamic association (C140). The data are consistent across both organisms and support a conserved function.

results.result: Conditional disruption of PfFRM2 resulted in complete abrogation of F-actin dynamics (from 92±5% to 5±4% cells with F-actin network), significant loss of viability, defects in apicoplast segregation, and dysmorphic parasites, with IPP supplementation failing to rescue viability indicating additional defects beyond apicoplast loss.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C73-C75, C141-C153 provide comprehensive evidence for PfFRM2's role in F-actin nucleation and apicoplast inheritance. Genetic excision (C141), protein loss (C143-C144), loss of F-actin network (C150-C152), apicoplast defects (C146-C147), and failure of IPP rescue (C148-C149) collectively support the conclusion. The inference of additional defects (C149) is well-justified by the IPP experiment.

results.result: PfFRM2 mediates efficient cytokinesis in P. falciparum, with conditional knockout resulting in reduced nuclei numbers, decreased fully segmented IMC (from 58±8% to 19±8%), and conjoined merozoites after egress, similar to PfACT1 knockout phenotypes.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C76, C156-C161 demonstrate PfFRM2's role in cytokinesis through multiple lines of evidence: reduced nuclear numbers (C156), IMC segmentation defects (C159), and conjoined merozoites (C160). The similarity to PfACT1 phenotypes (C160-C161) supports the conclusion that PfFRM2 and PfACT1 coordinate cytokinesis. This represents a species-specific function not observed in T. gondii.

results.result: PfFRM2 knockout parasites retained the ability to polymerize F-actin at the apical tip post-egress, indicating distinct non-overlapping functions for PfFRM1 (apical/invasion) and PfFRM2 (intracellular), consistent with prior reports of formin functional specialization.
results.evaluation: Claims C162-C163, C221-C223 demonstrate functional separation of formins through retention of apical F-actin polymerization in PfFRM2 cKO (C162, C221). This supports distinct localization-function relationships (C163, C223) and is consistent with prior work (C222). The data clearly show that loss of PfFRM2 does not affect all F-actin polymerization, indicating formin-specific functions.

results.result: Conditional disruption of TgFRM2 (excision in 36±4% of vacuoles) resulted in apicoplast segregation defects (65±7% of TgFRM2-negative parasites vs 1% baseline) and loss of the intracellular F-actin polymerization centre, while the intra-vacuolar F-actin network remained present and mitochondrial morphology was unaffected.
results.evaluation: Claims C168-C175 demonstrate TgFRM2's role in apicoplast inheritance and intracellular F-actin organization. Genetic excision (C168-C169), apicoplast defects (C170-C171), loss of polymerization centre (C174), persistence of intra-vacuolar network (C175), and normal mitochondria (C172) are well-documented. The persistence of the intra-vacuolar network distinguishes T. gondii from P. falciparum, likely due to Formin-3 (C176).

results.result: In T. gondii, TgFRM2 disruption resulted in loss of the dynamic intracellular actin polymerization centre and strongly reduced peripheral actin abundance, with kymograph analysis revealing loss of bi-directional actin flow along the parasite periphery, indicating TgFRM2 is a key regulator of actin distribution in intracellular parasites.
results.evaluation: Claims C178-C184, C188-C194 provide detailed characterization of TgFRM2's role in actin dynamics using time-averaged intensity profiling and kymograph analysis. Loss of the polymerization centre (C181), reduced peripheral actin (C182), disrupted bi-directional flow (C188, C194), and distinct phenotypes from TgAct and TgADF knockouts (C189-C193) support the conclusion that TgFRM2 is a major contributor to intracellular actin distribution (C183-C184, C219).

results.result: Formin-2 is the primary F-actin nucleator during intracellular growth in both P. falciparum and T. gondii, mediating apicoplast inheritance in both organisms and efficient cytokinesis specifically in P. falciparum, while Formin-1 functions during gliding and invasion.
results.evaluation: Claims C8, C196-C197, C206-C207, C209, C223-C226 synthesize the major findings showing Formin-2's conserved role in intracellular F-actin nucleation and apicoplast inheritance across both organisms, with species-specific involvement in P. falciparum cytokinesis. The evidence from conditional knockouts, localization studies, and functional analyses strongly supports these conclusions. The functional separation from Formin-1 (C223) is well-justified.

results.result: Kymograph analysis identified the apical and basal poles as additional sites of actin accumulation in T. gondii tachyzoites and revealed bi-directional actin flow along the cell periphery, with data suggesting these sites interact through a steady flow of actin allowing particle transport and exchange.
results.evaluation: Claims C213-C216 present novel findings on actin distribution and dynamics in T. gondii using kymograph analysis. Identification of apical/basal accumulation sites (C213), bi-directional flow (C214), and the proposed model of interconnected sites (C215-C216) are supported by experimental data. The model of steady actin flow (C216) is a reasonable inference from the observed dynamics, though the mechanism remains to be fully elucidated.

results.result: Super-resolution microscopy revealed a complex F-actin network in P. falciparum with prominent F-actin around the food vacuole (the basal end of newly-formed daughter parasites), showing time-averaged intensity peaks distinguishable from background and PfACT1 knockout parasites.
results.evaluation: Claims C102-C103, C105, C107, C120-C121, C195 demonstrate the spatial organization of F-actin in P. falciparum using super-resolution imaging and time-averaged intensity analysis. The complex network (C102), prominence around the FV (C103, C121), colocalization with actin antibody (C105, C107), and distinguishable peaks (C120) are well-documented. This provides important context for understanding Formin-2 function.

results.result: F-actin-rich peripheral accumulations were observed in ~60% of ring and early trophozoite stage parasites, showing highly dynamic changes in seconds that were disrupted by both cytochalasin-D and jasplakinolide, indicating requirement for dynamic F-actin regulation, and these were absent in PfFRM2 cKO parasites.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C91, C165 describe peripheral F-actin dynamics in early stages. The observations of dynamic accumulations (C86-C87), drug sensitivity (C88, C90), inference of dynamic regulation requirement (C91), and loss in PfFRM2 cKO (C165) are well-supported. However, the physiological relevance remains unclear as stated in the manuscript, limiting the significance of this finding.

results.result: CB-EME expression in gametocytes revealed intense dynamic F-actin structures at the tips and along the cell body, similar to previous antibody-based observations, forming an extensive network beneath the IMC, though chromobodies cannot distinguish between PfACT1 and actin-2.
results.evaluation: Claims C34, C98-C101 confirm and extend prior observations of F-actin in gametocytes using chromobodies. The dynamic network (C98), similarity to prior work (C99, C101), and technical limitation (C100) are clearly stated. This represents validation of the chromobody approach in a different life stage but does not provide major new biological insights beyond confirming prior antibody-based observations.

results.result: PfFRM2 punctae localized primarily with CB-EME-labelled filamentous structures (Pearson's R=0.36 vs 0.02 with DAPI), with 80±6% of individual PfFRM2-HA punctae closely apposed to the F-actin signal.
results.evaluation: Claims C154-C155 provide quantitative colocalization data supporting PfFRM2's association with F-actin structures. The Pearson's R value (C154) and manual counting (C155) are consistent and support the functional relationship. This is important supporting evidence for PfFRM2's role as an F-actin nucleator but is expected given the known function of formins.

results.result: TgFRM2-HA formed punctae on the CB-EME labelled F-actin network and appeared to colocalize with a polymerization centre, consistent with an independent report.
results.evaluation: Claims C166-C167 show TgFRM2 localization to F-actin and polymerization centres, consistent with Tosetti et al., 2019. This provides confirmatory evidence supporting the main findings but represents validation rather than novel discovery. The colocalization is expected given the known function of formins and the prior report.

results.result: Expression of chromobodies does not cause significant phenotypic effects (normal IMC marker staining) and allows reliable labelling of the F-actin cytoskeleton, enabling phenotypic probing of F-actin network state in vivo in a rapid and robust manner throughout growth, invasion, and in gametocytes.
results.evaluation: Claims C108-C109, C203-C204, C227 establish the validity and utility of the chromobody approach. Normal IMC staining (C108), lack of phenotypic effects (C109), and broad applicability (C204) support the conclusion. This is important methodological validation but represents technical rather than biological discovery. The claims are well-supported by the data presented.

results.result: Background claims establishing the biological context: P. falciparum actin is implicated in multiple cellular processes; malaria and toxoplasmosis cause significant disease burden; apicomplexan actins are divergent and form short unstable polymers in vitro; F-actin has conserved and divergent functions in P. falciparum and T. gondii including conserved roles in apicoplast inheritance but differences in invasion, egress, and cytokinesis requirements.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C9-C27 provide established background knowledge from prior literature, properly cited. These claims set the context for the current study and are well-supported by the cited references. They establish the rationale for the comparative approach and the need for F-actin visualization tools. These are not novel findings of the current study.

results.result: Background claims on parasite biology and prior actin research: P. falciparum expresses only actin-1 during asexual stages; parasites undergo distinct replication modes (endodyogeny vs schizogony) using conserved machinery; common actin probes don't work in apicomplexans but chromobodies were successful in T. gondii and bind P. falciparum actin in vitro; most actin regulatory proteins are missing in apicomplexans but two formins (FRM1 and FRM2) are present with prior reports of their involvement in invasion and apicoplast maintenance.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C71 provide essential background on parasite biology, actin expression patterns, replication modes, prior technical limitations, and formin biology. All claims are properly cited and establish the foundation for the current study. These represent established knowledge rather than novel findings, but are necessary context for interpreting the results.

results.result: Background and comparative context claims: Gametocytes express both actins and show F-actin along their length; formins possess FH1/FH2 domains that nucleate and elongate F-actin; Formin-3 is present in T. gondii but absent in P. falciparum and mediates intra-vacuolar network formation; TgFRM2 is expendable for invasion/gliding; prior studies reported non-overlapping formin functions; forces from actin polymerization can drive organelle segregation in other systems.
results.evaluation: Claims C96-C97, C125-C126, C176-C177, C185-C187, C210-C212, C217-C218, C220, C222 provide important comparative context and mechanistic background. These are properly cited and help explain differences between organisms (e.g., persistence of intra-vacuolar network in T. gondii due to Formin-3). They support the interpretation of results but are not novel findings of this study.

results.result: Speculative and future-looking claims: Prior inability to visualize F-actin restricted characterization; Formin-2 is speculated to be the main nucleator; PTEN-C2 domain likely used for apicoplast recruitment; diffuse TgFRM2 cKO kymographs likely due to peripheral actin and TgFRM1 contribution; apical polymerization likely mediated by Formin-1; chromobodies could be used for other parasite stages and to study other actin regulatory proteins.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C59-C60, C124, C134, C192, C202, C205, C208, C228 represent speculations, hypotheses, or future directions. While some are reasonable inferences from the data (e.g., C202 about Formin-1 mediating apical polymerization), others are explicitly speculative (e.g., C205, C228 about future applications). These claims are appropriately qualified in the manuscript but lack direct experimental support in the current study.

results.result: Integrative and summary claims: Prior PfACT1 characterization highlighted three primary functions correlating with chromobody findings; PfFRM1 was previously localized to invasion junction and PfFRM2 to cytosol; PfACT1 is required for normal cytokinesis; PfFRM2 cKO parasites reinvaded despite growth defects; TgFRM2-mediated actin nucleation is a major contributor to actin distribution in both organisms.
results.evaluation: Claims C122-C123, C158, C164, C198, C219 integrate current findings with prior work or provide summary statements. These are well-supported by the combination of current data and cited literature. They help synthesize the findings but represent integration rather than primary discoveries. The claims accurately reflect the data and prior knowledge.
